musique-concrete.d: Real-world sounds edited on magnetic tape into music, founded in Paris by Pierre Schaeffer; one of the starting points of electronic music.

elektronische-musik.d: The WDR studio in Cologne synthesized pure electronic tones from oscillators, the counterpart to musique concrète.

krautrock.d: German bands mixed rock, electronics, minimalism and improvisation; Kraftwerk travelled this line toward synth-pop.

ambient.d: Timbre and space replace melody and rhythm; Brian Eno defined it as music that must be able to be interrupted.

synth-pop.d: Post-punk synth bands carried disco's dancefloor feel and electronic timbres onto the pop charts.

downtempo.d: Nineties slow-motion electronica: breakbeat, ambient and soul mixed for sofas and headphones.

trip-hop.d: The Bristol sound: slow breakbeats, dark atmospheres and female vocals.

chillout.d: Soothing electronica made for the chillout room and the sunset.

idm.d: Electronic music made for headphones rather than the dancefloor: intricate beats and sound design.

synthwave.d: A retro imagining of 1980s film scores and synth-pop.

vaporwave.d: Eighties and nineties pop and advertising music slowed and chopped into a dream of consumerism.

rock-and-roll.d: R&B rhythm plus country guitar plus teenage rebellion; in the 1950s it split popular music in two.

rockabilly.d: Country singers taking on R&B: slapped bass, echo-laden guitar, wildcat vocals.

garage-rock.d: Rough rock recorded by amateur bands in garages, the spiritual ancestor of punk.

folk-rock.d: Folk lyrics and harmonies plugged into electric guitars; Bob Dylan and The Byrds were key.

psychedelic-rock.d: Feedback, echo, Eastern scales and studio experimentation simulate the psychedelic experience.

progressive-rock.d: Long-form pieces, concept albums and classical and jazz influence; rock written as symphony.

hard-rock.d: Louder, heavier blues rock: distorted guitars, power chords, big voices.

heavy-metal.d: Hard rock pushed darker and heavier: detuned guitars, double kick, occult and industrial imagery.

punk-rock.d: A reaction against progressive rock: short, fast, rough and DIY, putting rock back in the garage.

new-wave.d: Punk's energy plus synthesizers plus pop melody: the sound of 1980s radio.

post-punk.d: Darker and more experimental: funk bass, noisy guitar, cold-eyed lyrics.

gothic-rock.d: Post-punk's darkest branch: low voices, chorused guitars, vampire aesthetics.

industrial.d: Noise, metal percussion and tape experiments plus rock, later spawning industrial metal and industrial dance.

hardcore-punk.d: Punk sped up, weighted down and politicized, the common root of emo, post-hardcore and thrash.

thrash-metal.d: Heavy metal's speed plus hardcore punk's aggression, the starting point of Bay Area metal.

death-metal.d: Thrash taken to extremes: guttural growls, detuning, complex tempo shifts and technical playing.

black-metal.d: Extreme metal from the Norwegian underground: tremolo picking, shrieks, atmospheric darkness.

alternative-rock.d: An umbrella for underground rock, from college rock to grunge, that took over the mainstream in the 1990s.

shoegaze.d: Walls of guitar pedals and whispered vocals turn noise into a fog.

grunge.d: Seattle's muddy rock: metal's weight plus punk's grit plus a generation's gloom.

pop-punk.d: Punk speed plus pop choruses, mainstream on teen radio from the late 1990s through the 2000s.

emo.d: Emotional expression branching from hardcore punk: confessional lyrics, dynamic swells, later the black eyeliner.

post-hardcore.d: Hardcore's energy plus experimental structure, dynamics and melody.

post-rock.d: Rock instruments used for atmosphere and crescendo, vocals minimized, closer to classical narrative.

nu-metal.d: Heavy metal plus hip-hop rhythms plus detuned guitars, ruling the teen market around 2000.

metalcore.d: Hardcore punk plus death metal: breakdowns, double kick and melodic choruses.

pop.d: Songs written for the charts and the mass market: Tin Pan Alley's melodic tradition plus rock-era production.

dance-pop.d: Pop designed for radio and dancefloor at once: disco beats plus pop choruses.

city-pop.d: Pre-bubble Japan rendering funk, disco and soft rock as city nightscapes, rediscovered online in recent years.

teen-pop.d: Idol pop aimed at teenagers: dance beats, youth themes, the music-video industry.

electropop.d: The late-2000s synth-pop revival: sharp synthesizers, exaggerated vocals, club beats.

k-pop.d: Korea fused pop, R&B, hip-hop and the idol industry into a global phenomenon in the 2010s.

hyperpop.d: Pop, trap, electronics and internet memes pushed to the point of distortion.

son-cubano.d: Music of eastern Cuba: Spanish guitar, African rhythms and the tres, the skeleton of salsa.

mambo.d: Cuban son meets big-band jazz: brass riffs, syncopation, ballroom frenzy.

salsa.d: Cuban son plus New York Latin jazz plus Puerto Rican rhythms; the Fania label made it a global language.

cumbia.d: Dance music of the Colombian coast: accordion, guacharaca, steady bass, spread across Latin America.

ska.d: Jamaica sped up R&B and weighted the offbeats, the forerunner of reggae.

rocksteady.d: A transitional form after ska slowed down: heavier bass, more soulful vocals.

reggae.d: Slower and heavier on bass, with Rastafari and political consciousness; Bob Marley carried it to the world.

dub.d: Reggae stripped into echo and bass; King Tubby turned the mixing desk into an instrument.

dancehall.d: Digital riddims plus faster DJ chat, Jamaican dancehall culture.

reggaeton.d: Dancehall rhythm plus hip-hop plus Latin melody, built on the dembow pattern.

latin-trap.d: Trap's 808s and dark melodies plus Spanish, dominating global charts in the late 2010s.

highlife.d: West African dance-party music: guitar, brass and interlocking melodies, an influence on afrobeat.

afrobeat.d: Fela fused highlife, funk, jazz and political struggle into long, hypnotic, brass-driven pieces.

afrobeats.d: Modern Nigerian and Ghanaian pop: lighter and more melodic, spelled differently from afrobeat and sounding different too.
